newsitem.title: SPAIN: Short end of Spain yield curve could gain-dealers.
newsitem.headline: Short end of Spain yield curve could gain-dealers.

text.p: The short end of the Spanish yield curve could benefit in the next few weeks from an earlier-than-expected interest rate cut if the peseta gains further against the German mark, dealers said on Thursday.

"The Bank of Spain could be forced either to cut the official rate or to let the peseta gain ground against the German mark," said Francesco Giordano, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

Iberian bonds are seen treading water next week, with the 10-year spread over Bunds likely to stay glued to the current range of around 60-65 basis points for Spanish bonos and around 70 basis points for Portuguese bonds.

While the fact that the economy is picking up and analysts say inflation has bottomed out suggests that the Bank of Spain will hold its 5.25 percent key rate, a wide positive short term spread over German bonds is pushing the peseta higher versus the mark.
The dollar is at a 11-year high against the peseta but the mark has hit lows against the peseta since mid-April. At 1420 GMT, the peseta was trading at 84.18/21 per mark.

"I guess the Bank of Spain will resist a couple of months more. The economy is strong and the inflation already hit a record low. But the euro is a more important issue," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

Extensive intervention in the forex market by the Bank of Spain has shown up in currency reserves at the Bank of Spain, which rose by $956 million in June to $67.36 billion. That compares with $53.54 billion at the end of June 1996.
"But these massive interventions started to create problems for the central bank as money supply is formed in large amount by foreign currency," Giordano said.
In a few months, this intervention policy could cause problems in sterilising the money supply, leaving the central bank with only two alternatives -- cutting rates or letting the peseta strengthen.
"In one year's time the Spanish official rate has to be at least one full point lower from what it is now," he said.
At a Treasury auction on Wednesday, one-year and 18-month bill yields set a new record low at 4.951 percent on both maturities and dealers said the market could push lower.
The Spanish central bank has cut its key money rate 12 times since December 1995.
"And they will cut at least once more, by the end of September," Fernandez said.
But analysts predicted that the Bank of Spain would be interested in a less aggressive monetary easing policy as inflation seems unlikely to fall from current levels.
In June, Spain's consumer price index rose 1.6 percent year-on-year versus May's 1.5 percent increase.
Bank of Spain governor Luis Angel Rojo said on Wednesday that recent dollar strength had not so far suggested any danger that Spain's inflation would increase.
"Rojo's remarks yesterday are dangerous. It's not the first time he's tried to pour water on fears of inflation picking up," said Luca Jellinek, economist at Paribas in London.

Portugal's market is seen following its Spanish cousin, dealers said. The 10-year spread between the two markets, trading on Thursday at around 10 basis points, could shrink to around five or seven basis points, they said.
At the long end, dealers rule out big movements in the near future.
"The outlook remains positive the (10-year spread between Spanish bonds and Bunds) will head toward 50 basis points before the end of September," said Jellinek.
The Spanish bond market will be shut on Friday for a Madrid public holiday.
